1.1: 1.1 Argument. He extols Gaius for his piety, and exhorts him to remain in that same piety: he rebukes Diotrephes for impiety and pride. To Demetrius, however, he gives good testimony along with all the brethren.
1.2: 1.2 Concerning all things I pray, etc. As now right intention abounds in you, and the good will of giving to the needy continues, and the means of wealth, so may you always, by the Lord's help, be able to lead a life full of virtues.
1.4: 1.4 Greater than these. I rejoiced therefore, because I have no greater grace than that of these brethren coming, that is: when brethren come to me, in no deed or word of theirs do I rejoice more than when they announce that my children (whom I begot by preaching or baptizing) observe the truth of right faith and work.
1.5: 1.5 Beloved, you do faithfully, etc. Therefore you ought not to fail in hospitality and almsgiving. For whatever you do for the brethren faithfully, that is as a faithful man, that is as becomes the faithful, you do, not for vainglory, but show your faith by works.
1.7: 1.7 For for his name, etc. As if: They are truly to be honored, for they were not driven from their country for their crimes, but went out of their own will to spread the name of Christ, and to suffer for his name.
1.9: 1.9 I would have written perhaps, etc. You ought to persevere in almsgiving, because I perceive so great a profit in it that I would have written not only to you but to the whole Church about the commendation of almsgiving, but have dropped it by this necessity, because Diotrephes does not heed our authority. Diotrephes, the heresiarch of that time, by teaching new things usurped primacy to himself. Diotrephes is interpreted showily insipid, or raving beauty, so as to mark the perfidy of the heart even in the name. To the Church. To that Church which perhaps, that is doubtfully, is a Church, and that by the observance of almsgiving it might deserve to become a perfect Church, I would have written.
1.10: 1.10 I will put him in remembrance. That is, I will bring forth, in the knowledge of all, by rebuking more plainly; of whom he has no example anywhere; but he does these things, and invents new ones, prattling, using false reasons to confute us and so draw you back from the faith. As we ought not to stir up the tongues of detractors by our own fault, lest they perish, so we ought to bear evenly those stirred up by their own malice, that our merit may grow, and sometimes to restrain them, lest while they spread abroad things about us, they corrupt the hearts of those who could hear good things.
1.12: 1.12 To Demetrius testimony. Because he wishes to imitate the good, he opens it that he may imitate Demetrius, that with like praise he too may be worthy of all.
1.14: 1.14 Peace to you. He sends the grace of peace and health to friends, to show that the enemies of the truth are strangers to salvation.
